lesson.title: Downhill Chemistry: Exergonic Reactions and How Cells Put Them to Work
lesson.summary: Exergonic reactions are chemical reactions that release free energy and proceed spontaneously, and cells have evolved specific mechanisms to capture that released energy rather than letting it dissipate uselessly as heat.
lesson.body:
A reaction is called exergonic when it has a negative change in Gibbs free energy, meaning the products end up with less free energy than the reactants started with. That leftover free energy has to go somewhere, and in an exergonic reaction it is released to the surroundings, which is why these reactions are sometimes described loosely as energy-releasing or as proceeding downhill, by analogy to a ball rolling down a slope on its own rather than needing to be pushed up.

It is worth being precise about what spontaneous means here, because it is a common point of confusion. A negative delta G means a reaction is thermodynamically favorable and does not require a net energy input to proceed, but it says nothing about speed. Many exergonic reactions are extremely slow at normal biological temperatures because the reactant molecules need to absorb some initial energy, called the activation energy, before they can transform into products, even though the overall energy change still favors the products. This is exactly why cells are packed with enzymes: an enzyme lowers the activation energy barrier for a specific reaction without changing the delta G at all, so a thermodynamically favorable reaction that would otherwise take an impractically long time can instead happen fast enough to sustain life.

Cellular respiration is the clearest large-scale example of an exergonic process at work. Breaking glucose down into carbon dioxide and water is strongly exergonic, releasing a substantial amount of free energy overall, but the cell does not let that energy escape in one uncontrolled burst as heat. Instead, respiration proceeds through a long sequence of smaller enzyme-catalyzed steps, each one only mildly exergonic, so the energy is released in manageable increments that the cell can capture along the way, largely by using some of it to attach a phosphate group to ADP and generate ATP, rather than losing nearly all of it as heat in one uncontrollable step.

That captured energy does not stay idle. Because ATP hydrolysis is itself strongly exergonic, cells routinely couple it to reactions that are endergonic on their own, using the free energy released by breaking ATP's terminal phosphate bond to drive an otherwise unfavorable process forward, whether that is building a large molecule, transporting an ion against its concentration gradient, or powering the sliding of a motor protein along a cytoskeletal filament. In this sense, exergonic reactions are not just something that happens, they are the energy currency source that funds essentially every uphill, energy-requiring process a cell needs to carry out.

Stepping back, exergonic reactions are the practical, working expression of everything covered in this sequence: energy conservation from the first law shows up as the exact free energy released, the second law's push toward dispersal explains why some energy is inevitably lost as heat even in a well-run exergonic pathway, and the free energy framework from Gibbs is what allows a cell to identify, harness, and couple these downhill reactions with precision rather than by chance. From folding a protein correctly to beating a flagellum, nearly every organized, energy-demanding activity examined earlier in this unit is ultimately paid for by a coupled exergonic reaction somewhere in the background.
